routes.name: Atlantic triangle, leg 1: Liverpool to the Bight of Biafra
citations: Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1944)
Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (London, 1789) [public domain]
routes.notes: British slaving voyages carried trade goods to West Africa to buy captives. Shown from 1700 to the British abolition of the trade in 1807; other nations' trade ran earlier and later.
routes.goods_source: general history; not from a cargo manifest
routes.citation: Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1944)
routes.history: Liverpool and Bristol merchants moved into the African slave trade after the Royal African Company lost its monopoly in 1698. Ships left British ports loaded with manufactured goods, guns and ammunition, and textiles to buy captives on the West African coast. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807.
routes.story: This leg was the 'outward passage'. The goods carried on it were traded for people. The ship model shown is a stand-in East Indiaman. Real slave ships were usually smaller, purpose-fitted merchantmen.

routes.name: Atlantic triangle, leg 2: the Middle Passage
goods: enslaved African people, transported by force
citations: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (London, 1789) [public domain]
Marcus Rediker, The Slave Ship: A Human History (New York: Viking, 2007)
routes.notes: Captive Africans were shipped across the Atlantic in brutal conditions; many died on the voyage. Equiano, who survived it as a child, wrote one of the few first-hand accounts. Shown factually, with no game-like effects.
routes.citation: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (London, 1789) [public domain]
routes.history: The transatlantic slave trade carried off an estimated 12.5 million captives from Africa. About 10.7 million survived the crossing to the Americas. By the 19th century the Middle Passage took about five to seven weeks. Death rates varied widely, and on some voyages reached 47–58%.
routes.story: Olaudah Equiano, who was enslaved as a child, described the Middle Passage in 1789: the hold, the chains and the smell. His account became one of the key texts of the abolition campaign. This route is shown as a record of people, not as cargo.

routes.name: Atlantic triangle, leg 3: Jamaica to Liverpool
citations: Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1944)
routes.notes: Ships returned with plantation produce. Our line follows the Gulf Stream and westerlies.
routes.goods_source: general history; not from a cargo manifest
routes.citation: Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1944)
routes.history: On the last leg, ships carried sugar, rum and other plantation goods back to Britain. These goods were produced by enslaved labour in the Caribbean. Eric Williams argued that profits from this triangle helped finance British industry.
routes.story: The voyage home closed the triangle. Sugar from Jamaican plantations was unloaded at Liverpool docks, and the ship was fitted out again for Africa.
